newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: INTERVIEW-GM convincing managers on expansion.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-GM convincing managers on expansion.

text.p: The top executive of General Motors Corp's international operations said on Friday the U.S. carmaker has been winning over managers at its European units for the group's ambitious global expansion plan.

Louis Hughes, president of GM's international operations based in Zurich, told Reuters that GM should have done more in the past to convince workers of its commitment to European units Opel of Germany and British-based Vauxhall.

But he said recent surveys, including a comprehensive study done only two weeks ago, showed GM European managers are now throwing their support behind the plan after a series of meetings with managers to make clear the need for expansion.

"For me it has been a pure communication issue," Hughes said in an interview. "There is a gross misconception that we are taking hundreds, even tens, of German managers and putting them all over the world. That is not true."

"Our international expansion is only possible by preserving a strong Opel organisation and using the creative powers of our German engineering to create a product palate that we will sell to the world. All reports to the contrary are false," he said.

Hughes, who oversees all GM activities outside of North America, has launched the plan that calls for the U.S. carmaker to boost overseas output to five million vehicles a year over the next 10 years from about three million vehicles in 1996.

The plan calls for nearly identical plants to be built in Poland, Argentina, Brazil and Poland where GM will have flexible assembly capacity that will allow them each to produce two separate vehicle platforms and related models.

The new plants are based on Opel's plant in the east German city of Eisenach where Corsa subcompact models are built. Many of the new models will be based on Opel vehicles, which now account for two-thirds of GM's overseas output.

A report last June in the German news magazine Der Spiegel said an internal survey of top GM officials in Europe criticised the plan, saying the carmaker needed to devote more resources to European products and quality measures.

GM has also faced criticism in the German media over quality problems. It fears future models will lose their European appeal if U.S. engineers dominate the design process under GM's plan to use a handful of platforms to build cars.
The Detroit carmaker said in January that international profits may be flat or below the $1.53 billion they earned in 1996 due to weak European demand and expansion plan costs.
Opel, like Germany's Volkswagen AG and U.S. carmaker Ford Motor Co, has also seen its European market share erode this year and is under pressure to offer new products to regain lost sales.
Hughes, who believes GM must seize the opportunity to break into new markets, said Spiegel's reports about the survey were misleading since the study was completed last January.
He also said a recent comprehensive survey showed a strong majority of GM's European managers agreed with the strategy.

"We asked them specifically about whether they agreed or disagreed with our approach to globalisation. It showed that 88 percent of all of our managers agreed with the approach. I don't think anybody can get those kind of results," he said.

Hughes, a former Opel managing director, said GM, which suffered a decline in quality in the early 1990s, was starting to see improvements as a result of hiring hundreds of quality inspectors for its factories as well as key suppliers.

"The fact is that our quality improved but some of the competition improved faster," he said. "We have seen a really dramatic improvement in the quality numbers in the last year. But we will not give up until we are among the industry best."
Top GM officials have said the problems date back to component sourcing and manufacturing process decisions made in the 1980s and were unrelated to the global expansion plan.
"The key to this project is to take German engineering and build new products in these new plants," he said.
